chunks: And from him, from several of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Harun ibn al-Jahm, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

When the women migrated to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), a woman named Umm Habib migrated among them, and she was a 'khafidah' who would shave/cut the hair of the young girls. When the Messenger of Allah saw her, he said to her, 'O Umm Habib, the work that was in your hand is in your hand today.' She said, 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah, unless it is forbidden, in which case you would forbid me from it.' He said, 'No, rather it is permissible. Come closer to me so that I may teach you.' She came closer to him, and he said, 'O Umm Habib, when you do it, do not remove it completely (i.e., do not shave it entirely), but trim it, for it is brighter for the face and more pleasing to the husband.'

If it were shaved on the seventh day, it would be fine, because we have clarified previously that the 'Uqiqah (sacrifice for the newborn) is recommended, even if months and years have passed for the child. If the meaning of this report were not what we mentioned, the reports would contradict each other.

key_terms.أُمُّ حَبِيبٍ: Umm Habib, a companion known for her profession
key_terms.الْعَقِيقَة: The sacrifice made for a newborn child
key_terms.تَخْفِضُ الْجَوَارِيَ: She cuts/shaves the hair of young girls
key_terms.خَافِضَة: A female barber or hairdresser who cuts/shaves hair
key_terms.فَلاَ تَنْهَكِي: Do not remove it completely (do not shave entirely)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on shaving or trimming a girl's hair and its relation to the Uqiqah sacrifice?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) instructs Umm Habib, a female barber, to trim rather than completely shave the hair of young girls, noting that this practice enhances facial brightness and is more pleasing to the husband. The text reconciles this grooming advice with the tradition of *'Uqiqah* (sacrifice for the newborn), clarifying that the permissibility of trimming hair does not negate the recommendation of sacrifice, even if delayed. This narration highlights the Prophet’s attention to both aesthetic care and ritual continuity in early Islamic domestic life.
